Referencias: fichas planetarias de NASA; temperaturas de gigantes gaseosos al nivel de 1 bar.

Impact-monitoring records—rows in uploaded datasetEach row is one possible impact date/solution in the saved Sentry export, not necessarily a different asteroid.
Highest listed probability——The largest probability in any single row. It is not the combined chance across all rows.
Impact energy range—megatonnes (Mt)Estimated energy if an impact occurred; 1 Mt is equivalent to one million tons of TNT.
Torino Scale—all records in this fileA public 0–10 hazard communication scale. 0 means no unusual level of concern; higher values indicate greater concern.

Highest individual impact probabilities

Top 10 records ranked by the probability listed for each date. Probabilities are not added together.

Probability means the estimated chance for the specific impact scenario shown in one row. A value such as 0.01% is a one-in-10,000 chance for that scenario; it is not a prediction that an impact will happen.

Dataset overview

Quick definitions: median is the middle value after sorting; Palermo Scale compares a scenario's risk with the background risk from objects of similar size.

The uploaded file does not include an asteroid name or usable Earth-distance / impact-width values. Those fields are intentionally shown as unavailable. Palermo values are logarithmic comparisons with background risk; Torino values are a separate 0–10 public communication scale.

How to read the columns: Potential impact date = the modeled date of a possible encounter; Probability = chance for that row's scenario; Energy (Mt) = estimated impact energy; Palermo = technical comparison against background impact risk (negative values are below background); Torino = 0–10 public hazard scale. Click a row to see more fields.

Scientific note: This is an analysis of a saved Sentry monitoring export, not a live risk assessment. Each probability belongs to an individual listed date/solution. Do not sum the probabilities: the records may be related solutions for the same object. A Torino Scale of 0 means the listed scenario is below the scale's threshold for concern; it does not mean the object has zero probability. The CSV does not identify the asteroid, so this dashboard does not assign it a name.

HELICENTRIC ORBIT · TOP VIEWScale: AU

How to read this map: The Sun is at the center. The blue dashed circle is Earth's 1 AU orbit. The orange curve is the selected asteroid's calculated orbit; the orange dot is its position at the chosen date. AU (astronomical unit) is the average Earth–Sun distance, about 150 million km. This is a top-down 2D view, so inclination above/below Earth's orbital plane is not visible here.

Sun Earth's orbit (1 AU) Selected asteroid Asteroid orbit
Choose an asteroid to inspect its orbital elements.

Why are these called NEO candidates? This local subset was selected using perihelion distance q < 1.3 AU. That means the orbit comes within 1.3 times Earth's average distance from the Sun at its closest point. It is a catalog filter, not proof of an Earth crossing or collision risk.

Model limitations: The plotted path is calculated from the catalog's osculating Keplerian elements at epoch 2026-09-17. It is a two-body approximation, not an N-body ephemeris; it does not include planetary perturbations or predict an Earth impact. The catalog's perihelion-distance filter q < 1.3 AU is used to select near-Earth-object candidates. It does not mean these objects are on a collision course.

Data: Lowell Observatory's astorb.dat. Catalog attribution: Lowell Observatory endowment and NASA PDART grant NNX16AG52G. About the astorb database.
